content: 1. The individual signing this document agrees not to disclose the discussions or decisions made during the meetings of the Joint Meeting on Pesticide Specifications (JMPS) to anyone outside these meetings unless explicitly agreed upon by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Health Organization (WHO). 2. The obligations outlined in this document will remain binding on the individual even after their responsibilities related to the JMPS have ended. 3. The individual agrees to return all copies of any information provided by FAO and/or WHO, depending on the source of the information, promptly after the JMPS has completed its review of the material. 4. Nothing in this agreement or any related document shall be interpreted as a waiver of the privileges and immunities of FAO and/or WHO. (Note: Temporary advisors or experts on mission are entitled to certain privileges and immunities.) 5. Any disputes regarding the interpretation or application of this agreement, unless resolved amicably, will be subject to conciliation under the Conciliation Rules of the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL) currently in force. If conciliation fails, the dispute will be resolved through arbitration, conducted in accordance with the Arbitration Rules of UNCITRAL. The parties involved must accept the arbitration award as the final resolution of the dispute. 6. A letter of access to confidential data is required during the development of FAO/WHO pesticide specifications. This letter ensures that the confidential data on manufacturing processes, purity, and impurities provided in support of the technical material for a proposed FAO/WHO specification is consistent with the data assessed by a competent authority for pesticide registration. 7. The purpose of the letter of access, provided by the company, is to allow the appointed evaluator and the registration authority to assess the similarity of the data and communicate with the evaluator. The letter must include full contact details of the company and the national authority, as well as the registration number to facilitate access to national files. 8. The calculations used by WHO/PCS to advise JMPS are based on known concentrations of the active ingredient and impurities in the technical material, as well as their toxicological properties (e.g., LD50, ADI, BMD, NOAEL, LOAEL). These calculations apply the dose-additivity model, as synergistic effects at low exposure levels are rare, and dose-additivity is recommended as a worst-case scenario. 9. The maximal acceptable concentration of an impurity in the technical material is calculated to ensure that the increase in toxicity of the technical material does not exceed 10%. If multiple impurities are relevant, their total acceptable concentrations are calculated based on their relative toxicities. 10. Examples are provided to illustrate the calculation of acceptable impurity concentrations and their relevance based on toxicity and manufacturing quality control limits. These examples demonstrate how the impurity's toxicity and concentration are assessed in relation to the technical material's purity and toxicity. 11. Solid mixtures cannot be perfectly blended, and the dispersion of analytical results depends on the size of the test portion analyzed. Therefore, the test portion size must be defined in the specification for a blend of solids. Expanded tolerances for such blends are empirically calculated based on achievable manufacturing, sampling, and analytical variations. 12. The FAO and WHO jointly develop pesticide specifications to provide robust and universally applicable standards for pesticide quality. This collaboration is based on a Memorandum of Understanding between the two organizations. 13. The March 2016 revision of the first edition of the Manual on the development and use of FAO and WHO specifications for pesticides supersedes previous versions and provides standardized processes, unified requirements, harmonized definitions, and technical guidelines for pesticides used in agriculture and public health. 14. FAO/WHO specifications apply only to products from manufacturers whose technical materials have been evaluated. These specifications serve as an international reference for judging product quality, aiding regulatory and commercial purposes, and preventing the trade and use of inferior pesticide products. 15. By enhancing confidence in pesticide quality, these specifications contribute to improved pest control, sound agricultural production, effective vector control, and better safety for users, the public, and the environment, particularly in developing countries.
